newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian PM unveils austerity budget for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian PM unveils austerity budget for 1997.

text.p: Bulgaria's Prime Minister Ivan Kostov on Friday unveiled to parliament an austere 1997 budget, promising that the government would sustain its restrictions throughout the operation of a currency board system.
"This budget reflects the grim condition of Bulgaria's economy today. This is a budget of harsh financial restrictions ... the first one tailored to the operation of a currency board," said Kostov.
Bulgaria is due to launch the self-regulating restrictive monetary mechanism on July 1 as part of reform pledges to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Kostov said there was no time limit for the system.

"The currency board in Bulgaria will not end. From this system, Bulgaria will enter the European Union and will become part of European monetary union," he said, echoing economists' views that the system's restrictions will bring Bulgaria close to the targets for joining the single European currency.

Kostov warned deputies who favour higher social spending that exceeding the rigid budget framework would put the country in a disastrous situation where it would have to operate a currency board without external support.

"No one should allow this budget to fall through. If we do not adhere to this budget we will violate the agreements with international financial institutions," said Kostov, referring to Bulgaria's history of revising budget spending several times a year.

The budget, to be voted on item by item in two readings until the end of the month, envisages a deficit equal to 6.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) which is assumed at 16.15 trillion levs ($9.6 billion).
GDP is expected to fall by a real 7.4 percent from 1996. GDP fell a real 10.9 percent last year.
The budget envisages a fixed exchange rate of 1,000 levs to the mark as part of the currency board system, which requires that levs in circulation be matched by foreign exchange reserves.
"For the first time in seven years we are able to offer businesses in the country sufficient stability to plan their costs and investment for the long term," said Kostov.
"The (exchange) rate will remain 1,000 levs per mark this year, and for two years...until the peg will change to a different unit of the European currency system," he added.
Bulgaria's economy went in to a tailspin in February when the lev nosedived in one week from 600 per dollar to more than 3,000.
Foreign debt interest payments due this year account for 2.9 percent of GDP and domestic debt interest due is assumed at 6.9 percent of GDP.
Social security payments were assumed at 1.577 trillion levs, defence was allocated 390 billion levs, the interior ministry 222 billion levs and the state health service 469 billion levs.

A bomb threat telephoned to parliament interrupted Finance Minister Muravei Radev's presentation of the budget after Kostov's speech but most deputies and top government officials ignored it. The interior ministry said it was a false alarm.

Kostov said that opponents of the currency board who wanted to continue siphoning state funds into private companies were doomed to fail. The currency board system bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks.
"Failing this budget will place Bulgaria in the position of a man with a rope around his neck kicking away the chair beneath his feet," said Kostov.
